Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, Advocate, Mozammel Huq Khan, Advocate, instructed by A. Rab-II, Advocate-on-Record-For the Appellant.
Jani Alam, Senior Advocate, instructed by S.M. Huq, Advocate-on-Record-For Respondent No. 1.
Ex-parte—Respondents No. 2-4.
parties:
Akrab Ali and others  ------- Appellants.
Vs.
Zahiruddin Kari and others  ------- Respondents.
case_source: (From the Judgment and Decree dated 23.1.1974 passed by the High Court Division in S.A. No. 35 of 1973.)
full_judgment:
Debesh Chandra Bhattacharya J. - This appeal by special leave is against a judgment of a Bench of the High Court Division, allowing a Second Appeal and restoring the judgment and decree of the trial Court by which a suit for declaration of title and for recovery of possession of certain lands, brought by Respondent No.1, was decreed.

2. Respondent No.1 instituted the suit on the allegations that the disputed land originally belonged to one Aftabuddin Sarkar, who gave the land in usufructuary mortgage to one Fdizuddin Haji for a period of three years for a sum of Rs. 50/-. After expiry of the said period Aftabuddin Sarkar got back possession of the land and possessed it till his death. After his death the land devolved upon his son Nawab Ali as his only heir. Nawab Ali died leaving three sons including the plaintiff and three daughters as heirs and on amicable partition amongst the heirs the plaintiff alone got the disputed land in his share and had been in possession as such. The defendants claiming to have purchased the land from the heirs of Faizuddin Haji on 6-1-66 started disturbing the possession of the plaintiff, whereupon certain criminal cases were brought against the defendants and the suit is stated to have been insti-tuted to remove the cloud which had been cast upon the plaintiff's title to the disputed land because of the claim of the defendants.

3. The suit was contested by Appellant No.1 and the predecessor of the remaining appellants contending, inter alia, that Faizuddin Haji purchased the disputed land from Aftabuddin Sarkar for a sum of Rs. 50/- and got delivery of possession of the said land before C.S. operation and accordingly the name of Faizuddin Haji was recorded in the C.S. Khatian, that the story of usufructuary mortgage in respect of the disputed land, as alleged by the plaintiff, was not correct, that Nawab Ali, the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiff, taking advantage of the long distance of the residence of Faizuddin Haji and his heirs from the disputed land got his name fraudulently recorded in the S A. Khatian though they had no right, title or possession in the same. The contesting defendants having purchased the disputed lands from the heirs of Faizuddin Haji, the rightful owners, by two registered Kabalas the plaintiffs were not entitled to any relief as against them.

4. The trial Court decreed the suit on the finding that Faizuddin Haji was merely a usufructuary mortgagee in respect of the disputed land for a period of three years only, on the expiry of which Aftabuddin Sarkar resumed possession and possessed the land till his death and that after the death of Aftabuddin Sarkar the land devolved upon Nawab Ali, after whose death the plaintiff obtained the land exclusively in his share on the basis of an amicable partition with his co-sharers.

5. On appeal the Second Court of the Additional District Judge, Dacca, reversed the findings of the trial Court on holding that Faizuddin Haji acquired the right, title and interest in respect of the disputed land by virtue of an oral purchase from Aftabuddin Sarkar, the original owner of the said land, as had been correctly recorded in the C.S. Khatian, that Faizuddin Haji and after his death, his heirs possessed the disputed land and that thereafter Defendants No.1 and 2 came into possession of the said land by virtue of the purchase made from the heirs of Faizuddin Haji.

6. In the Second Appeal preferred by Respondent No.1 the learned Judges of the High Court Division reversed the findings of the Court of appeal below on the view that the contesting defendants having admitted the title of Aftabuddin Sarkar, the plaintiff's predecessor and the entry in the C.S. Khatian having merely proved the possession of Faizuddin Haji, the defendants failed to discharge the onus of proof that Faizuddin Haji acquired title to the disputed land by a purchase of the same.

7. Special Leave was granted by the Appellate Division for considering the points: (1) whether the High Court Division wrongly placed the onus of proof of title and possession upon the defendants and (2) whether the High Court Division committed any illegality in disturbing in the second appeal the findings of fact as to possession as arrived at by the first appellate court on the basis of the C.S. Khatian.

8. Mr. Khandker Mahbubuddin Ahmed, learned Counsel, has submitted that the learned Additional District Judge having come to the finding on a consideration of the evidence and the circumstances of the case, on reversing the finding of the trial Court that the plaintiff had failed to prove that Aftabuddin Sarkar mortgaged the suit land to Faizuddin Haji and that the presumption of the C.S Khatian Ext. A that Haji Fiizuddin purchased the land from Aftabuddin Sarkar, the original owner of the disputed land, for a valuable consideration stood unrebutted, the learned Judges of the High Court Division committed a substantial error of law in shifting the onus of proof on the contesting defendants on a mistaken view that the said defendants admitted the title of the plaintiff's predecessor and that the entry in the C S. Khatian did not raise any presumption as to Faizuddin Haji's acquisition of title by purchase, Learned Counsel for the appellant has further submitted that the learned Additional District Judge having come to the conclusion on an analysis of the oral evidence adduced by the parties that the evidence of P.Ws. who were incompetent and interested persons, could not be believed and having accepted that of the D.Ws as reliable, the learned Judges of the High Court Division exceeded their jurisdiction, conferred by section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure, in interfering with the finding of possession of the disputed land arrived at by the learned Additional District Judge, the last Court of fact.

<u>9. Mr. Jani Alam, learned Counsel appearing for the Respondent, has on the other hand contended that having regard to the pleadings of the parties and the evidence adduced in the case the learned Judges of the High Court Division were correct in their view as to the presumption raised by the entries in the settlement records of right as also the defendants failure to discharge the onus of proof as to their predecessors title to the disputed land. The settlement Khatian No.680 of Mouza Dahsin Khan, which has been marked as Ext. A, has recorded the plot No.1873 measuring 1-84 acre as "Jote Afiabuddin Sarkar, occupant Faizuddin Haji by purchase at Rs. 50/-"; in the column of the tenancy it has been described as the right of a settled raiyat and in the column of 'rent' a remark has been recorded to the effect "fit for rent but no transaction". The Cadastral Survey records of right were finally published in the district of Dacca before the amendment of Bengal Tenancy Act in 1929 when any transfer of an occupancy raiyati holding or a part thereof was made compulsorily registrable irrespective of the fact whether the consideration was above or below Rs. 100/-. Before such amendment, according to section 17 of the Registration Act, only those transfers which were for a consideration of Rs. 100/- and above were compulsorily registrable Therefore, the purchase of the land appertaining to C.S plot No.1873 by Faizuddin Haji from Aftabuddin Sarkar for a price of Rs.50/-did not require under the law then in force a registered instrument and could have been made orally. In those days, of course, every transfer, whether by a registered deed or otherwise, was subject to the consent of the landlord but for which the purchaser's right of tenancy was not entitled to be recognised by the landlord. In the absence of such consent the purchase was not binding upon the landlord although it was binding upon the rest of the world. From the entries of the Khatian Ext. A it appears to be clear that Faizuddin Haji got into occupation of the land by virtue of his purchase for a consideration of Rs. 50/- from Aftabuddin Sarkar, the original holder of the jote, who was a settled raiyat of the village, but no rent appears to have been fixed because an agreement with the landlord as to the amount of rent was not perhaps concluded by that time. The name of Faizuddin Haji was recorded as an occupant by purchase and the class of the tenancy was stated to be that of a settled raiyat and the remark in the column for rent was that it was assessable to rent but no amount of rent was mentioned as there was no transaction. The question which has been debated is whether from such entries a presumption to the title or the right of tenancy of the recorded person can be made. According to section 103 (B) (5) of The Bengal Tenancy Act every entry in a record of rights finally published shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. The learned Judges of the High Court appear to have started with the view that the Court of appeal below was palpably wrong in presuming title in favour of the defendants from a mere entry in the records of right and that the defence having admitted title of the predecessor of the plaintiff, the plaintiff was relieved of the burden of proving the title of Aftabuddin Sarkar. Their Lordships were not correct in their view as to the effect of the entries in a finally published record of right and in relieving the plaintiff, in the face of the said entries of the burden of proving the title of Aftabuddin Sarkar. The entries in the Khatian Ext. A that Faizuddin Haji was in the occupation of the holding appertaining to the jote of Aftabuddin Sarkar on the basis of purchase for a consideration of Rs. 50/- and that the land was fit for assessment of rent but there was no payment were not beyond the scope of the survey held under Chapter X Part 1 of the Bengal Tenancy Act, 1885. According to section 102 of the said Chapter, the particulars to be recorded in such a survey "may include, either without or with any edition to other particular, some or all of the following, namely, (a) the name of each tenant or occupant (b) the class or classes to which each tenant belongs that is to say, whether he is a tenure holder, raiyat holding at a fixed rate, settled raiyat, occupancy raiyat, non-occupancy or under raiyat.....(c) the situation and quantity and one or more of the boundaries of the land held by each tenant or occupier (d) the name of each tenant's landlord...........(e) the rent payable at the time the record of rights is being prepared… (h) the special condition and incident, if any, of the tenancy......(i) if the land is claimed to be rent free....whether or not rent is actually paid, and, if not paid, whether or not the occupant is entitled to hold the land without payment of rent, and if so entitled, under what authority........</u>

10. From the said provisions it is clear that the authority in charge of survey had to record all the particulars and incidents relating to the right of the person in possession of all lands in any local area, estate or tenure in respect of which the survey had been ordered under section 101 of the Act. It is the record of rights, and not the record of mere possession or occupation, which was to be prepared under Chapter X. The term itself seems to be self-expressive, Sir Lawrence Jenkins in delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee of Privy Council in the case of Dakas Khan Vs. Ghulam Khan Qasim ILR 45 Cal 793 28 C L.J. 441 explained the nature of an entry in a record of right, as is generally understood; in the following words:

"A record of rights has been described by Sir Henry Maine as a detailed statement of all rights in land drawn up periodically by the functionaries employed in setting the claims of the Government to its shares of the rental........

Though it does not create a title, it gives rise to a presumption in its support, which prevails until its correctness is successfully impugned".

<u>11. The relevant entries in the settlement record of rights are that Faizuddin Haji was in occupation of the disputed holding, that the nature of his occupation was that of a purchaser from Aftabuddin Sarkar, who was a settled raiyat of the village, for a consideration of Rs. 50/- and that although no payment was made the tenancy was liable to assessment of rent. These entries were not beyond the scope of the survey which was held under the aforesaid Chapter X of Bengal Tenancy Act and as such the presumption as the correctness of the said entries necessarily arose by virtue of sub-section (5) of section 103 B of the Act. The plaintiff having come to the Court with the allegation the entry as to Faizuddin Haji's occupation of the holding as a purchaser was wrong and that he was led into occupation of the said holding as usufructuary mortgagee for a period of three years only, the burden of proof was undoubtedly upon him to show that the entry as to the purchase was wrong and that the transaction in question was really one of usufructuary mortgage. The defence case is that the transaction was really an oral sale for a consideration of Rs. 50/- and direct evidence was adduced in this regard by one Waris Dariji, aged 80 years, who was examined as D.W.2. Such a transaction having taken place before the introduction of section 26C by the Bengal Tenancy (Amendment) Act 1928, there was no bar to an oral sale of an occupancy holding if the consideration did not exceed Rs. 99/-. No evidence could be produced by the plaintiff to rebut the presumption raised by the entries in Ext A. The trial Court held in favour of the plaintiff’s title on the view that there had been a subsequent record of rights prepared under the provision of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, where the plaintiff's predecessor has been recorded as the tenant in occupation and that the later record superseded the entry of the earlier record. It should be pointed out that no finally published record of rights under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act with regard to the disputed holding was filed in the case although a provisional record of rights showing Nawab Ali, the predecessor of the plaintiff in occupation of the holding, has been proved in the case and marked Ext.2. Such a document has no presumptive value whatsoever. As a matter of fact, in the plaint there is no allegation as to the subsequent record of right indicating a contrary state of affairs. The cause of action as alleged in the plaint was stated to be 6-1-66, being the date of the defendant’s first purchase. It is in the written statement of the defendant’s that a reference to the later record of right showing the name of Nawab Ali in possession of the disputed land was made on the allegation that such an entry was brought into existence by taking advantage of the absence of the heirs Faizuddin Haji from the locality. Under section 144A which was introduced by the East Pakistan Ordinance No. VIII of 1967 every entry in a record of rights prepared or revised, under section 144 shall be evidence of the matter referred to in such entry and shall be presumed to be correct until it is proved to be incorrect. The record of rights referred to in the said section is one which is prepared or revised under section 144 i.e. to say which has been finally published under sub-section (7) of the said section. No record of right which was finally published under sub-section (7) of section 144 having been adduced in evidence as has been pointed out by the learned Additional District Judge, the question of presumption under section 144A of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act does not arise in this case.</u>

12. Even if it had been a finally published record of right under the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act showing the predecessor of the plaintiff to be in occupation of the disputed holding, that would not have ipso facto rebutted the presumption raised by the entries in the earlier record of right. According to law, both the record of right shall be presumed to be correct at the respective dates of their final publication. Whether the presumption of correctness of the entries in the particular record of right has been rebutted or not shall have to be decided with reference to the facts and circumstances in each case. The later record of right will merely show that the plaintiff's predecessor was the raiyat or tenant at the date of the final publication of the later record and the entry in the earlier record will show that the original holder of the tenancy namely, Aftabuddin Sarkar, the predecessor of Nowab Ali, who has been subsequently recorded as tenant transferred his interest by way of said sale and thereby lost his interest in the tenancy. The question whether the presumption of correctness of the earlier record takes away the foundation of the entry in the later record and thereby nullifies the presumption arising therefrom or whether the subsequent record mentioning the right of tenancy of the plaintiff's predecessor will show that the earlier record of rights showing the occupation of Faizuddin Haji as a purchaser rather than as a mortgagee to be incorrect will depend upon the evidence adduced in the case.

13. It may be noticed that at the date of the cause of action of the suit or at the time when the dispute arose between the patties there appears to have been no such record of rights. That is to say, in January, 1966 apparently there was no record of rights containing an entry in support of the tenancy right of the plaintiff's predecessor nor there was at that time any law attaching any presumptive value to the entries in the record of right prepared under the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The defendants have no doubt admitted that the holding in question formerly belonged to Aftabuddin Sarkar but they having made out a case that Faizuddin Haji had acquired the interest of Aftabuddin by purchase and that the C.S. Record of rights having recorded the name of Faizuddin Haji as an occupant by purchase of the holding the learned Judges of the High Court Division were clearly wrong in deciding the case on the view that there was no presumption of title in favour of the defendant's predecessor and that the plaintiff was relieved of the burden of proving the title of Aftabuddin Sarkar.

14. The next question for which special leave was granted is with regard to the extent and scope of the jurisdiction of the High Court Division to interfere with a finding of fact arrived at by the Court of appeal below, the last Court of fact In the absence of any error of law or error of procedure affecting the merits of the case the High Court Division is bound by any finding of fact, however erroneous it may appear to the High Court Division in respect of the appreciation of the evidence on which the said finding is based. Under Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure the High Court Division can interfere with a finding of fact of the Court of appeal below only when such a finding is vitiated by an error of law or procedure. The learned Judges of the High Court Division have proceeded to decide the case on the view that all that could be presumed on the basis of the C.S. record was that Faizuddin Haji was in possession at the time when the C.S. Khatian was prepared and that the defence having admitted the title of Aftabuddin Sarker the onus was on the defendants to show that Faizuddin Haji got this land on the basis of sale and that they having failed to do so, the admitted title of the plaintiff could not be defeated.

15. We have already pointed out that the learned Judges were not correct in their view as to the onus of proof in the case. But apart from the presumption arising from the entries in the record of rights, there is direct and positive evidence as to the acquisition of title to the disputed land by Faizuddin Haji by virtue of an oral purchase for a consideration of Rs. 50/- from Aftabuddin Sarkar, which was believed by the learned Additional District Judge and to which the attention of the learned Judges of the High Court Division does not appear to have been drawn.

16. Learned Additional District Judge of the Court of appeal below after considering the evidence of D.W.2 accepted the same with the following observation:

"D.W.2 Waris Darjeeis an old man of 80 or 85 years. He has got land to the southwest corner of the suit land. He proves that the suit land belonged to Mahtabuddin Sarkar (i.e. another name of Aftabuddin Sarkar) who sold the same to Faizuddin for Rs. 50/- and he further proves that Faizuddin Hajee possessed the suit land himself and he also possessed through bargadars. He states that defendants 1 and 4 have been in possession of the suit land for the last 4/5 years and the plaintiff or his brothers or his father never possessed the suit land. He is a disinterested and clearly a man of the locality and I see no reason to disbelieve his version."

17. After observing that the finally published S.A. Khatian was not before the Court he proceeded to record the finding that Faizuddin Haji possessed the suit land as a purchaser of the same. The learned Judges of the High Court Division do not appear to have noticed this finding on the Question of the title and possession of Faizuddin Haji.

18. On the question of possession the learned Judges referred to the evidence of defence witnesses on whom the Court of appeal below placed its reliance and expressed the view that the said Court totally overlooked the fact that the evidence of possession given by the said witnesses was in favour of the defendants who are purchasers and who came on the land sometime in 1965-66 and that none of the sons or nephews of Haji Faizuddin or their bargadars having been examined, the assertion of defence witnesses on the question of possession prior to the defendant’s coming upon the land could not be accepted and that the trial Judge was justified in discarding their evidence on this account. The learned Judges clearly treated on the prohibited area of assessment of evidence. The learned Additional District Judge examined the evidence of each and every witness separately and came to the view that the plaintiff's witnesses, namely, P.W.1 being the plaintiff himself, P.W.5 being highly interested and P.W.6 being a full brother of the plaintiff and P.Ws. 2, 3 and 4 being not competent witnesses in respect of possession could not be relied upon and that the defence witnesses, namely, D.Ws. 2, 3, 4 and 5 being disinterested men of the locality there was no reason to disbelieve their version and ultimately the learned Additional District Judge came to the following finding:

"It appears from the certified copy of the attested S.A. Khatian Ext.3 that the name of Nawab Ali was recorded and a few rent receipts Ext.2 series have been filed to show payment of rent by Nawab Ali to the Govt. But I find no basis for entering the name of Nawab Ali in this S.A. Khatian. The finally published S.A. Khatian is not before the Court. Any way these provisional rent receipts were made available since Nawab Ali could manage to get his name entered in the S.A Khatian. But in the face of above facts and evidences on record I have reason to find that the defence version of the case 10 the effect that Faizuddin Haji possessed suit land as purchaser of the land and after him his heirs possessed the same and after that the defendants 1 and 2 came into possession of the suit land by virtue of purchase is true and I hold that the plaintiff has not acquired any right, title and interest in the suit land."

<u>19. The learned Judges of the High Court Division nave refused to accept this finding on the view that certain witnesses were not examined support of the defence case of possession. Any adverse inference which may be drawn from the non-examination of a witness is a question relating to the probability of a fact, as has been mentioned as an illustration to the provision of section 114, under which the Court may presume the existence of any fact which he thinks likely to have happened, regard being had to the common course of natural events, human conduct and public and private business in their relation to the facts of a particular case. The illustration (g) of the said Section specifically deals with the question and it provides that the Court may presume that the evidence which could be and is not produced would, if produced, be un-favourable to the person who withholds it. This making of adverse presumption under section 114 of the Evidence Act is not obligatory upon a Court but it is in its discretion to make such a presumption, depending upon the facts of a case. It is essentially a question of fact and it is for a Court of fact to decide whether in the facts of a particular case such a presumption would be drawn. Moreover, the evidence, as has been referred to in the said illustration, must be of such a nature as was within the power of the party to produce and was not produced because of his withholding the same. The sons and nephews of Faizuddin Haji or their bargadars cannot certainly be said to have been under the control of the defendants and could not be examined in Court because the defendants withheld them. The learned Additional District Judge having come to the view on an analysis of the evidence adduced by the parties in the case that the evidence given by the plaintiff's witnesses could not be believed and the evidence adduced by defence witnesses No.2, 3, 4 and 5 were trustworthy and the finding on the question of title and possession of the disputed land being based upon such view of the evidence, such a finding, in the absence of legal or procedural error, was binding upon the High Court Division. The High Court Division exceeded their jurisdiction as conferred under section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure in disturbing the said finding.</u>

<u>The result, therefore, is that this appeal is allowed. The judgment and decree of the High Court Division are set aside and those of the Court of Additional District Judge are restored, but there shall be no order as to costs.</u>

End.
